name: Seleucid Empire
summary: The largest Hellenistic kingdom formed from Alexander’s empire, founded by Seleucus I. It spread Greek culture from Syria to Iran until Rome annexed its last lands in 63 BCE.

location.value: Syria, Mesopotamia, Iran and at first Central Asia.

terrain.value: Mediterranean coast, river plains and the Iranian plateau.
terrain.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

climate.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

resources.value: Rich farmland of Mesopotamia and Syria, and trade.
resources.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

disasters.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

urbanisation.value: Founded Greek-style cities: Antioch, Seleucia on the Tigris, and many others.

disease.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

migration.value: Greek and Macedonian settlers came to new cities.
migration.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

economicBase.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

tradeRoutes.value: Routes between the Mediterranean, India and Central Asia.
tradeRoutes.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.
wealth.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

inequality.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

keyRulers.value: Seleucus I (305–281 BCE), Antiochus I, Antiochus III the Great (223–187 BCE), Antiochus IV.

institutions.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

armyAndTech.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

majorWars.value: Battle of Ipsus (301 BCE), Roman–Seleucid War and Magnesia (190 BCE), Maccabean Revolt (167–160 BCE).

territoryChange.value: About 3.9 million km² in 301 BCE, shrinking to 100,000 km² by 100 BCE.

scienceEducation.source: Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

openness.value: Greek culture spread among local elites.

riseSignals.value: Seleucus I took Babylon in 312 BCE.

peakPeriod.value: Around 301 BCE, after the Battle of Ipsus, and again briefly under Antiochus III.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Seleucid Empire (checked 6 Nov 2026); Kosmin, The Land of the Elephant Kings (2014)

declineSignals.value: Defeat at Magnesia and losses to Parthia.

outcome.value: Annexed by Rome under Pompey in 63 BCE.

sources.value: Greek historians, inscriptions, coins. Checked against Wikipedia (“Seleucid Empire”).

overallCertainty.value: Good for major events; known mostly from Greek and Roman writers.
